title: Akara
author: Jemimah Ogunleye
desc: Beans blended thick, then whisked ten minutes — or stirred vigorously in one direction for ten to twelve — and fried at about 180°C for three to four minutes.
longDesc: Akara is the deep-fried bean fritter eaten at breakfast across Nigeria, and like every bean dish in the repertoire it lives or dies on air. The batter is blended thick, deliberately short of water, then beaten until it is very fluffy — and the instruction here is specific in a way that matters: if you are using a wooden spoon, stir vigorously in ONE direction for ten to twelve minutes. The peppers are folded in at the end, lightly, so the air you worked in does not come straight back out.
equipment: Deep pan or pot for frying
steps: Pick and wash the beans, then soak 5 minutes in lukewarm water and peel — pour into the blender and pulse a couple of times so the skins come off, then finish by hand.
Blend the peeled beans till smooth in a mill or electric blender. Do not add too much water; you need to end up with a thickish consistency.
Blend the bell pepper, onion and scotch bonnet roughly with as little water as you can. Sieve if there is excess water.
Incorporate air into the batter. Whisk for at least 10 minutes till it becomes very fluffy, or use a wooden spoon and stir vigorously in one direction for 10 to 12 minutes.
Add the blended pepper, bouillon cubes, ground pepper and salt. Mix lightly, or just fold the pepper in — do not over-mix or you will lose the air you have worked up.
Scoop the batter in and fry till golden brown, about 3 to 4 minutes, turning them over for even frying.
chefTips: One direction, if you are using a spoon. Ten to twelve minutes, always the same way round. Changing direction knocks the air back out.
Thickish batter. Too much water and the akara will spread and absorb oil instead of puffing.
Fold the peppers in. The beating is finished by then and the mixing from here is only to distribute.
180°C. Cooler and they soak up oil; hotter and the outside colours before the inside sets.
Five minutes in lukewarm water is all the soak the beans need before peeling — and note this author soaks for ten for her moin moin, without explaining why.
Sieve the pepper blend if it is wet. Water in the batter is water in the oil.
Eaten with hot pap, custard or oatmeal in the morning, or with soft white bread — agege bread (NGA036) is the classic partner.
commonMistakes: Stirring back and forth instead of one way.
A batter loose enough to pour.
Over-mixing after the peppers go in.
Frying in oil that is not hot enough.
Crowding the pan, which drops the oil temperature.
sources: Adapted from 'Akara – Bean Fritters', byline Sisi Jemimah. Quantities as printed: 3 Cups Brown or White Beans, Vegetable Oil for frying, 1 Red Bell Pepper (Tatashe), 1 Scotch Bonnet (Atarodo), 1 Medium Size Onion, 1 Tablespoon Ground Pepper/Atagungun (Optional), 2 Knorr Cubes, salt to taste.

THE AERATION INSTRUCTION, verbatim and the reason this version is used: 'Incorporate air into your Akara batter. The air helps with the fluffiness and plumpness of Akara. You can use a whisk for this, whisk for at least 10 minutes till the batter becomes very fluffy or you can use a wooden spoon and stir vigorously in one direction for 10-12 minutes.' And on folding: 'Mix lightly or just fold the pepper in with the batter, do not over mix or you'll end up losing the air you've worked up.'
Frying as printed: 'heat the oil to approximately 180 degrees'; 'Fry till golden brown, this should take 3-4 minutes. Remember to turn them over for even frying.' Yield not specified.
The batter consistency instruction is hers: 'Do not add too much water. You'll need to end up with a thickish consistency.'
DISAGREEMENT within one author's work on the bean soak: 5 minutes in lukewarm water here, 10 minutes for her moin moin (NGA022). She gives no reason for the difference.

Note the aeration triad across her three bean recipes, which is consistent with the textures each dish wants: akara, whisk 10 minutes or wooden spoon in one direction 10 to 12 minutes; moin moin, mixer 8 minutes plus 5; ekuru, hand mixer 10 to 15 minutes or wooden spoon 30 minutes. Ekuru gets by far the most work.
Her headnote also records the Brazilian connection: akara 'is also known as Acarajé by Brazilians although the Brazilian recipe calls for the addition of shrimps to the batter'. See NGA029.
storage: Best within the hour. A day refrigerated at most.
reheating: 5 minutes in a hot oven or air fryer. Never the microwave, which makes them soggy.
healthBenefits: Cowpeas are high in plant protein, folate and soluble fibre.
No wheat, no dairy, no egg.
Low glycaemic index despite the frying.
A good source of iron and potassium.
culturalNote: Akara is breakfast and it is street food, sold from a single wide pan at the roadside from before dawn. It crossed the Atlantic with enslaved West Africans and became acarajé in Bahia, where it is fried in dendê — palm oil — rather than vegetable oil, and received Brazilian heritage status in 2004. In the north the same fritter is kosai, and the Hausa version is eaten with koko rather than pap.
